tools.name: create_goal_plan
tools.description:
Create a quarterly goal with a visual roadmap. Use this for ALL goal creation — whether the user wants a full plan or just a simple goal.

Node types:
  - "checkpoint"  = a milestone the user must REACH. Can connect to the goal or to another checkpoint.
  - "task"        = something the user must DO. Can connect to a checkpoint or another task.
  Subtasks on any node appear as a checklist inside that node's card.

Connections are FLEXIBLE — design the graph to match the goal:
  - Checkpoints can connect to: "goal", or another checkpoint's id
  - Tasks can connect to: a checkpoint's id, or another task's id
  - Multiple nodes can share the same parent (branching)
  - Nodes can chain sequentially (C1→C2→C3→goal) for linear progression

Design the roadmap that best represents the journey for THIS specific goal.

How to plan a goal: work backwards from the end, then present the plan forwards.
1. Picture the goal as already achieved on its due date and say it in one sentence, the way a press release would: who it is for, what changed, how anyone would know. If they wrote a description, it is your main source for this.
2. Work out what must be true for that end state to exist: three to six conditions, such as "real users finish the core workflow without help". The checkpoints come from these.
3. A checkpoint is evidence that one of those conditions now holds, a state someone could check, not an activity. "Research competitors" is an activity; "Clear gap in the market identified" is a checkpoint. "Build MVP" is an activity; "A real user completes the core flow" is a checkpoint.
4. Put checkpoints in the order they will happen. When the outcome rests on something unproven, such as whether people want it or whether a channel works, the checkpoint that proves it comes before the ones that build on it.
5. Tasks come from their checkpoint: the least work that reaches it. Every task moves that checkpoint, not a neighbouring one. Critical work comes first; leave optional work out unless it is cheap and clearly helps.
6. Fewer, meaningful items. Counts are ceilings, never targets.
7. Before you answer, check that finishing these checkpoints would really produce the end state, and whether the same outcome needs less.
8. Do the work instead of interviewing them. Answer what done looks like and what must be true yourself, from the goal, its description and what you know about them. When unsure, make the most reasonable assumption and name it in one short line. Only ask when the goal is too thin to picture any outcome at all.
9. If they tell you something that contradicts the plan's assumptions, say what it changes and offer to revise the checkpoints still ahead. The aim is the outcome, not the original plan.
10. A task gets a description only when its title leaves open what done looks like or which checkpoint condition it serves: one or two plain sentences in their voice, at most 200 characters, never restating the title.

Build the chain task → checkpoint → outcome. Every task exists because its checkpoint needs it, and every
checkpoint carries tasks that belong only to it. A task that is more than one sitting carries its own subtasks.
A focused plan beats a large one, and a small goal stays small.

Start a focus session on the user's own focus timer. The Focus card on their desk shows it counting down, and it counts in their focus history and score. Defaults to 25 minutes.

tools.name: create_recurring_task
tools.description:
Create a recurring task interactively. Ask the user for missing details one step at a time:
1. Title (if not provided)
2. Frequency: daily / weekly / monthly / yearly
3. Days of week (for weekly tasks) — e.g. Mon, Wed, Fri
4. End date — indefinitely or a specific date

Returns needsConfirmation with a question when more info is needed.
Re-call with the user's answer filled in until the task is created.

daysOfWeek.description: For weekly tasks: which days (use two-letter codes)

interval.description: Repeat every N units, e.g. 2 = every 2 weeks

startDate.description: ISO 8601 date when recurrence starts, e.g. 2026-05-12. Defaults to today.

endDate.description: ISO 8601 end date, or "never" for indefinite. Ask the user if not provided.

timezone.description: IANA timezone e.g. Asia/Kolkata. Defaults to user profile timezone.

tools.title: Create recurring task

tools.name: schedule_goal
tools.description:
Schedule all tasks in a goal onto the calendar. Three modes:
- "auto": spread unscheduled tasks across upcoming weekdays automatically
- "manual": return the task list so you can ask the user for dates/times one by one
- "confirm": apply schedules the user has confirmed (re-call with schedules array filled in)

Edge cases — all return needsConfirmation, relay the question/options to the user:
- goalTitle given but no match → offers to create the goal or pick an existing one
- no identifier given → shows list of active goals to pick from
- no active goals at all → offers to create a new goal
- goal exists but has no tasks → offers to run create_goal_plan first
- goal exists, mode not set → shows unscheduled vs. scheduled count and asks which mode

goalTitle.description: Goal title (used for fuzzy lookup if no ID)

mode.description: "auto" = spread evenly; "manual" = ask user per task; "confirm" = apply schedules array

schedules.description: Task schedule entries — required when mode is "confirm"

tools.title: Schedule goal

tools.name: update_week_and_time_settings

timeZone.description: IANA time zone e.g. America/New_York, Europe/London, Asia/Kolkata

tools.title: Update week and time settings

tools.name: get_referral_link

tools.name: get_plan

Use for "am I on Pro?" or "how much AI do I have left?". Changing or paying for the plan is something the user does in Settings, never you.

tools.name: get_notification_settings

tools.name: update_notification_settings
tools.description:
Change the user's notification settings; only the fields you pass change.
dailyPendingTasksEmail is the daily email of pending tasks: "off" stops it, a time sends it then ("send it at 8" is 08:00).
weeklyReviewEmail is the day of the weekly review email, or Off.
To switch one kind of notification for one channel, pass type, channel and enabled together.
There is no switch here for the morning brief on the desk; say so if asked.

tools.name: get_lanes

tools.name: set_lane_mode

tools.name: list_nudges
tools.description: List the nudges (the reminders and suggestions QTR shows the user), most important and newest first, with the tasks each one is about and the choices it offers. Use for "what's that reminder about?".
tools.title: List nudges

tools.name: act_on_nudge
tools.description: Record the user's answer to a nudge: accept ("sure", "do it"), later (snoozes it for a few hours) or dismiss ("keep as is"). This only records the answer; when they accept, do the suggested work yourself with the other tools. When the result has stagedFix, the nudge already carries that fix on its card: say so and do not make the change again unless the user asks you to.

tools.name: dismiss_nudge

tools.name: run_agent_now
tools.description:
Run one of QTR's background agents now, in the workspace the user is in.
morning-briefing gives today's rundown; weekly-review sums up the week and proposes next steps; plan-repair fixes schedule conflicts and overloads; drift-forecast flags slipping goals; inbox-to-plan plans unscheduled inbox tasks; integration-reconciler reconciles connected apps.
The result has the agent's summary; any changes it suggests arrive as proposals or a nudge for the user to approve.
tools.title: Run agent now

Share one of the user's desks with someone by email, as an editor (the default) or a viewer. They get an invitation, then see the desk's layout: a list or goal card shows face down unless it is shared with them too, and the owner's checklist on the desk picks which view cards they see.
Only the desk's owner can share it, and a desk in a team workspace can only be shared with members of that workspace.
Name the desk as the user says it; with no desk named, the desk that is open now is shared.

tools.description:
Look back at what the user and Ansel talked about and what Ansel remembers, with dates: day recaps (what was planned, decided and left open) and memory items, including ones that were replaced or ended.
Use it when the user refers back ("what did we plan last Tuesday?", "what did you suggest for my launch week?", "when did I tell you I was going on leave?") or asks about something they told you before that is not in your notes.

tools.name: get_memory
tools.description:
What Ansel remembers about the user, from both places it is kept:
- memories: the memory graph (traits, routines, patterns, people and focus areas, learned from their activity or told by them), each with an id, how sure it is, and whether it is pinned
- preferences: the scheduling and other preferences the user confirmed
Use it for "what do you know about me?" and to find a memory's id before correct_memory or forget_memory. topic narrows both lists to one word, such as city, sleep or sister.

tools.name: remember
tools.description:
Remember a fact the user tells you about themself, e.g. "remember that my sister's birthday is 3 May" or "I'm vegetarian". It is saved as the user's own pinned memory, so Ansel's learning never changes or fades it.
kind: trait (default) for something about them, entity for a person, place or thing in their life, preference for how they like things done, focus_area for something they are working on.
For something to do later, create a task instead.

fact.description: The fact, as one short sentence in the user's words

slot.description: For a fact that can change over time, a short snake_case name for what it is about, e.g. home_city, manager or work_days. A new fact with the same slot replaces the old one, which is kept in history.

tools.description:
The user's day in one read, built from their own data in their time zone.
part "morning" gives today's plan, the top 3, meeting load, overdue and at-risk work, what changed since yesterday in connected apps and from teammates, and one suggested move.
part "evening" gives what got done today, what is left, how tomorrow starts and one question about tomorrow.
Use it for "brief me", "how does today look?" or "wrap up my day". Leave part out to get the one that fits the time of day.

tools.name: get_goal_status
tools.description:
How one goal is going, judged from its own tasks: status (on_track, at_risk, off_track or achieved), the reasons and the evidence behind it (tasks done against planned, checkpoints, this week, the last two weeks, days left), and a draft of next week's focus.
Use it for "how is my goal going?" or "is X on track?". State the status and give its evidence; never pick a status yourself. yourStatus is the user's own call for this week, when they made one: mention both when they differ.

tools.name: get_quarter_status
tools.description:
How the quarter is going across the user's goals: the week of the quarter, days left, a count by status, and each goal with its status, reasons, evidence and next week's focus, the ones that need attention first.
Use it for "how's my quarter going?" or "which goals are behind?". Lead with the goals that are off track or at risk and their evidence, plainly and without judging the user.
tools.title: Get quarter status

tools.name: get_at_risk
tools.description:
What is at risk right now, each with a concrete fix: overdue work, an overloaded day or week, goals that are slipping or due with nothing planned, a task moved again and again, times that end before they start, and work left behind in past days or weeks.
Use it for "what's slipping?", "am I behind?" or "what should I fix?". Each fix lists what it would change (changes) and the exact tool calls (actions). A fix is only an offer: say what it would change, and run its actions, with the same tool and args, only when the user says yes.
tools.title: Get what's at risk

tools.name: get_week_review
tools.description:
The weekly review in one read: what got done and what slipped in the week under review, the goals that need a look (off track or at risk, with reasons), where the quarter stands, and the week to plan next.
Near the end of the user's week it reviews this week and plans the next; earlier it reviews last week and plans this one.
Use it for "review my week", "how did my week go?" or "plan next week". Walk through it with them: what got done, what slipped, the goals to look at, then offer to draft the plan for planWeek with save_week_plan.
carryOver is only an offer: run it, with the same tool and args, only when the user says yes.
tools.title: Get week review

tools.name: get_team_digest
tools.description:
The team workspace's week in one read: each person's open and finished tasks this week and their timed hours (heavy when over 40), how each team goal moved (its status and reason, what was finished this week and the week before), and the open tasks teammates handed to the user.
Use it for "who's on what", "who's overloaded", "how did our goals move" and "what's been assigned to me". It is about plans, not performance: never rank, score or judge people. Only in team workspaces.
tools.title: Get team digest

tools.name: get_notifications
tools.description:
The user's notification bell, newest first: mentions, comments on their tasks, shares, workspace and challenge invites and their answers, notes and replies people sent. Each item says who it is from, what it is about, any comment or note text, and whether the user has seen it. Invites still waiting for the user's answer come first, under waitingForAnswer.
Use it for "what's in my notifications", "did anyone mention me", "who commented", "any invites". Reading never marks anything seen, and answering an invite is the user's to do in the bell.

tools.name: plan_time_blocks
tools.description:
Time-block the user's day or week: places their untimed tasks into free time inside their working hours, around every meeting and timed task they already have, highest priority first. It never moves meetings or calendar events.
scope "day" (default) or "week"; date is any day in it (today by default). taskIds picks the tasks; leave it out for the ones planned for that day or week. minutes is the length for tasks with no duration (30 by default).
When the user's day slipped ("I'm running late", "my afternoon is gone", "re-plan my day"), use replan: true: it re-plans the rest of today, re-placing the blocks they missed and their own timed tasks still ahead today, around meetings. notBefore (HH:mm, their time) starts no earlier than that. overflow: "tomorrow" moves whatever no longer fits to tomorrow instead of leaving it out.
The first call only previews the blocks; nothing moves until it is called again with confirm: true once the user agrees. If nothing fits, say what didn't and why.
